svg.title: How the Richmond–Petersburg Turnpike came to be built through Jackson Ward, Richmond, 1946 to 1958
svg.desc: 1946: Harland Bartholomew and Associates' master plan for the city, made for the City Planning Commission, proposes expressways through it. (Encyclopedia Virginia (the plan); Style Weekly, 2013. Wikipedia, citing Campbell, names R. Stuart Royer and Associates as the firm that proposed a turnpike) June 13, 1950: Voters reject the expressway plan in a citywide referendum. Only 8 of 55 precincts vote for it. (Style Weekly, 2013; Rogers, 2011, quoting Silver) November 1951: A second referendum, forced by former mayor J. Fulmer Bright's petition, fails by almost 2 to 1. A headline of the day put the margin at 6,002 votes. (Style Weekly, 2013; Rogers, 2011 (the same writer), citing the Times-Dispatch. His notes on Silver give June 13, 1951) August 24, 1953: City Council, 6 to 1, concurs in a consultant's report on toll roads for the Richmond–Petersburg area. Silver writes that this moved the decision to the General Assembly and prevented another referendum. (Rogers, 2011, from the Council's records and quoting Silver, p. 192 (the book not seen)) April 8, 1954: The General Assembly creates the Richmond–Petersburg Turnpike Authority, with the power of eminent domain. The act lets the Authority fix the road's location, subject to the State Highway Commission, and puts its powers beyond any city's supervision. (Acts of Assembly, 1954, ch. 705. Library of Virginia, Wikipedia and VCU give 1955 for the Authority) About four months later: The Authority announces that the road will run through Jackson Ward. (Campbell, 2012, p. 154, as cited by Wikipedia (the book not seen)) 1955–1958: Clearance and construction. The Authority photographs the work monthly, 1956–58. In 1956 Sixth Mount Zion Baptist Church is spared. (Community Plan, 2026; Library of Virginia, 2024; DHR nomination, 1996) July 1, 1958: The Turnpike opens: 34.7 miles, $76.7 million, paid for by toll revenue bonds. In August it becomes part of I-95. (Library of Virginia, 2024; Wikipedia)
